newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest hog movement seen slowed by fieldwork.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest hog movement seen slowed by fieldwork.

text.p: U.S. Midwest hog marketings were seen slowing by mid-April as spring fieldwork coincides with a seasonal decline in market-ready hogs, livestock analysts said.

"In another week, or so, we will be getting into field preparation for planting, and there just are not going to be as many hogs ready for slaughter in absolute terms, than what we saw during the month of March," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst with Alaron Trading Corp.
Levitt added that the hog cycle has evened out in recent years as more hogs are raised in environmentally-controlled confinement buildings, but seasonal factors still exist.
The seasonal reduction in hog supplies starts about mid-April and goes until a low point is hit sometime during July, Levitt said.
This year should be no exception as hog numbers start thinning this spring, said Dave Maher, analyst with Securities Corp of Iowa.
"I think you'll see the regular seasonal, with a few more hogs hitting the market as they (producers) try to get things cleaned up before we get into planting," Maher said.

The extra marketings could swell daily interior Iowa/southern Minnesota hog receipts to 115,000 to 120,000 head, or more, as producers try to get current before concentrating fully on fieldwork, Maher said.

Alaron's Levitt estimated weekly slaughter to peak this spring near 1.825 million head within the next two weeks before declining by about 50,000 per week starting the week that ends April 26, which he estimated at 1.775 million.

Hog slaughter last week was estimated by the U.S. Agriculture Department at 1.717 million head, but was 100,000 short because of Easter holiday plant closings on Monday, Levitt said. Slaughter this week should be close to 1.820 million head, Levitt said.
"The low point in the slaughter will come in June or July and should be down around 1.5 million (head)," Levitt said.
While hog marketings may follow the usual seasonal trend this year, prices may not. Hog prices will likely move higher than usual this year, buoyed by increased export demand from Japan, Maher said.
Japan's largest pork supplier, Taiwan, announced March 20 that it was out of the export market for an indefinite period due to an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in its hog herd.
The news caught world pork markets by surprise and heightened ideas that U.S. pork was the most likely to replace most of the lost Taiwan pork business, market watchers said.
"Price outlooks are a little higher with people thinking Japan," Maher said.

Maher said he raised his average May price outlook to $58.00 per cwt from $56.50 for hogs sold in Iowa/southern Minnesota direct trade. Maher also raised his June outlook to $62.00 from $57.00 and his July outlook on Iowa hogs shifted to $61.00 from $55.00. Maher sees the average August price at $59.00 versus his previous outlook for $52.00.
"That's all providing we get the business from Japan," Maher said. "For the near term, I think we'll probably hold around $55.00 for the next couple of weeks," he said.

Interior Iowa/southern Minnesota barrow and gilt prices were steady to $1.00 higher early Monday, with a top of $53.50 paid on hogs delivered to the plant, USDA reported. Daily hog marketings there were estimated at 100,000 head, above 79,000 a week ago and 98,000 a year ago, USDA said.
